intro: Bank of England averages for 2-year fixed mortgage rates by deposit size, what moves them, and how they relate to Bank Rate and the average paid on newly-drawn mortgages.
explanation:
## The averages show advertised rates, not the rate you would get

The 2-year fixed figures on this page are Bank of England averages of the rates UK lenders advertise. There is one for each deposit size. Deposit size matters because lenders price by **loan-to-value**, which compares what you borrow with what the property is worth. A 5% deposit means borrowing 95% of the value, and a 25% deposit means borrowing 75%.

An average of advertised rates is a market benchmark. The rate a lender offers you depends on its own range, the loan-to-value band you fall into, your circumstances and any product fees. The averages do not include those fees.

## Three different rates are easy to confuse

The page shows three kinds of figure, and they measure different things.

- **Bank Rate** is the interest rate the Bank of England sets. It is decided by the Monetary Policy Committee, which meets eight times a year. It is not a mortgage rate.
- **Advertised 2-year fixed rates** are what lenders say they will charge on the fixed-rate deals they're offering. They are averaged by loan-to-value band.
- **The average rate on newly-drawn mortgages** is what the Bank calls the "effective" rate: the interest actually being paid on mortgages taken out in the month. It covers newly drawn mortgages in general, so it is not specific to 2-year fixes.

The three are measured differently, so their figures differ.

## A fixed rate does not follow Bank Rate during the fixed period

A 2-year fixed rate stays the same for the whole fixed period, whatever happens to Bank Rate in that time. When the period ends, a mortgage that has not been moved to another deal goes onto the lender's reversion rate, which is often its standard variable rate. The rate on a replacement deal is whatever is on offer at that point.

## What moves 2-year fixed rates

Lenders do not set fixed rates from Bank Rate alone. The Bank of England tracks quoted 2-year fixed mortgage rates against the two-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate, a market rate that reflects what is expected for Bank Rate over that time, along with a premium for risk. Rises in this reference rate can pass through to quoted mortgage rates relatively quickly. That is why a 2-year fixed rate can move before Bank Rate does, or without Bank Rate moving at all.

## Why a 5-year fix is shown for comparison

The page also shows the average 5-year fixed rate at the 75% loan-to-value band, so you can set it beside the 2-year average at the same deposit size. The two terms differ in how long the rate is locked in. A 2-year fix means the mortgage reaches the end of its fixed period, and the next rate is set, sooner than with a 5-year fix.

The Bank of England averages on this page cover the whole UK. In Scotland a mortgage is also known as a standard security, and the legal steps around it follow Scottish rules, such as registering a discharge when it is paid off.
